title: Do You Feel Guilty When Taking Time Off?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The Admired Leadership newsletter examines why so many leaders feel guilty taking time off, tracing it to three overlapping causes: leaders who inflate their own indispensability by centralizing decisions and communication, leaders who fear missing critical opportunities while away, and leaders who worry that disconnecting will read as a lack of commitment in 'always on' cultures. The piece argues all three stem from a shared attachment to control and to how leaders are perceived by others, not from a genuine business need. It warns that when leaders model constant availability, their teams absorb the same anxiety, extending the dysfunction downward through the organization. The article closes by linking real rest to better decision-making and creativity, urging leaders to confront the actual psychological source of their guilt rather than simply working through vacations.
points: Identifies three root causes of vacation guilt: manufactured indispensability, fear of missing key decisions, and pressure to appear 'always on.'
Argues leaders who hoard decision-making create the very dependency that then justifies their guilt about leaving.
Notes that leaders who never disconnect implicitly pressure their teams to do the same, spreading the anxiety organization-wide.
Frames disconnecting as a performance and well-being issue for the whole team, not just a personal indulgence for the leader.
Closes by tying meaningful breaks to better decision-making and creativity, reframing rest as a leadership skill.
quotes: Feeling guilty about taking time off is so common among leaders that it can almost be categorized as a disease.
Far too often, the guilt leaders feel prevents them either from taking the time off they should or from enjoying the experience when they do.
When leaders see themselves as indispensable, they come to believe the team can't function properly without them.
Sadly, leaders often manufacture their centrality by controlling decisions, communication, and workflow.
For leaders who thrive on the action, missing key deals, decisions, or opportunities can become a source of anxiety.

Three sources of guilt, but one underlying pattern. The leader who hoards decisions, the leader who can't stop checking their phone, and the leader who performs availability for the culture all share a debilitating attachment to control and how they are seen.
Until leaders come to grips with the true source of their guilt and learn to overcome that guilt, everyone suffers — families, teams, and entire organizations.
